name: Snowball Earth
statement: At times in the deep past, ice may have spread from the poles all the way to the equator, freezing the whole planet.
statementAccent: all the way to the equator
meaning: The Snowball Earth hypothesis proposes that at one or more times in the deep past, Earth's surface became entirely or very nearly entirely frozen, with glacial ice reaching sea level in the tropics during episodes of severe global glaciation. The events most often meant fall in the Cryogenian Period, roughly 720 to 635 million years ago, comprising the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations, with an earlier Paleoproterozoic candidate in the Huronian glaciation. The hard version, a fully ice-covered planet, is debated against a slushball alternative in which a band of open water persisted at the equator.
mechanism: Onset is driven by the ice-albedo feedback: ice and snow reflect sunlight, cooling the planet and growing more ice, and once ice advances to within about thirty degrees of the equator the feedback runs away to a global freeze. Escape comes from carbon dioxide. With the ocean ice-covered, the silicate weathering that normally removes carbon dioxide largely shuts down while volcanoes keep outgassing, so carbon dioxide builds up over millions of years to enormous levels until an extreme greenhouse melts the ice abruptly. The hot aftermath precipitates distinctive cap carbonates over the glacial deposits.

examples.text: Glacial deposits are found at low paleolatitudes, within about ten degrees of the equator by paleomagnetic evidence, the central and most striking sign that ice once reached the tropics.
A commonly sharp transition from glacial deposits directly into thick chemically precipitated limestone or dolomite records the rapid greenhouse aftermath of a global melt.
The competing model holds that a band of thin ice or open water remained near the equator, preserving a hydrological cycle and a refuge for photosynthetic life.

variants.name: Sturtian and Marinoan
variants.text: The two great Cryogenian glaciations, the Sturtian lasting from about 717 to 660 million years ago and the Marinoan ending around 635 million years ago, the events most geoscientists mean by Snowball Earth.

variants.name: Slushball Earth
variants.text: The variant in which the equatorial ocean did not freeze solid, important because open water sustains the water cycle and a refuge for life through the glaciation.

whyItMatters: Snowball Earth episodes bracket a pivotal interval in the history of life. The severe icehouse-to-hothouse cycles are thought to have imposed intense evolutionary bottlenecks and pressures, with the emergence of complex multicellular life in the Ediacaran following soon after the Marinoan deglaciation and, later, the Cambrian explosion. It also reshaped the oceans and atmosphere, returning banded iron formations under long-lived ice cover and leaving large carbon-isotope excursions, making it a key episode in Earth-system history.

working.text: read a global freeze as the ice-albedo feedback passing a tropical tipping point, not as a gradual cooling.
expect carbon dioxide to accumulate under the ice until an extreme greenhouse melts it abruptly, leaving cap carbonates behind.
treat the extent of ice cover as the open question, since a surviving band of equatorial water changes how life persisted.

limits: The hard, fully frozen form is contested; the extent of ice cover, global versus near-global with an open equatorial belt, is the core dispute, and modelling and isotopic evidence have led many to favour a partly open ocean. The survival of life, especially photosynthesisers, is a central challenge, since total ice cover would cut off sunlight to the oceans, prompting proposed refugia at hydrothermal vents, meltwater ponds, and pockets of liquid water. Dating remains uncertain, particularly the Marinoan onset and whether the earlier Huronian truly reached snowball conditions, so the severe low-latitude glaciations are accepted while their full extent is not.
misreadings: It is not established that the whole Earth was definitely frozen solid; that is the contested strong claim, and slushball scenarios remain viable. It did not happen only once: there were at least two Cryogenian events plus the earlier Huronian candidate. Carbon dioxide did not cause the freeze; long-term carbon-dioxide buildup is the proposed escape from it, while the freeze is driven by the ice-albedo runaway. Kirschvink did not invent the whole idea; he coined the name and supplied the escape mechanism, building on earlier low-latitude glaciation evidence and albedo modelling. And life clearly persisted through these events.
origin: The term was coined by Joseph Kirschvink in 1992, who added the carbon-dioxide escape mechanism, building on W. Brian Harland's 1960s evidence for low-latitude glaciation and Mikhail Budyko's ice-albedo modelling; the modern synthesis was developed by Paul Hoffman and Daniel Schrag around 1998.

sources.text: Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson, and Schrag, 'A Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth,' Science 281 (1998): 1342-1346. — the modern hypothesis, cap carbonates, and the carbon-isotope evidence.
